title: The Case of the Missing Spice Bun
markdown:
Gadzooks! In a village of cheerful cottages and flowers lived Pebble the pantry rat, Coral the parrot, and Moss the goat — the gentlest, fluffiest creature you ever did see.

Every Tuesday Granny Buttercup baked spice buns: warm, gooey, spiced so perfectly they made whiskers twitch. Pebble peeked through a bakery knothole just to breathe the aroma. Coral, from the eaves, shrieked, “Spice buns. Spice buns. Warm and yummy.” Moss always got a crumb from kind Granny Buttercup.

One sunny Tuesday, after a glorious batch cooled, Pebble saw a plump bun simply vanish. Poof. Gone in a blink.

“Crikey,” he squeaked. “Coral. Moss. We have a situation.”

Coral swooshed down. “Did the oven go bang?” Moss ambled. “What’s wrong, little friend?”

Pebble vibrated. “The spice buns. One missing. And there were only four left.”

Coral gasped. “This is a bun-eruption.”

Moss tilted his head. “Who would take a bun without asking?”

Pebble declared a sting operation: playful, paw-some, completely harmless. Coral wanted a disguise. Moss munched clover and asked how.

Task one: the decoy. “Coral, pretend to be a very tempting, slightly overripe banana.”

She puffed. “I can be a magnificent banana. Beware, bun-nabber.” She did a wobbly colourful banana sway that would have fooled a fruit bowl and confused a king.

Task two: the statue. “Moss, silent guardian behind the oak. Imposing. A very large, very quiet statue.”

Moss gave a gentle moo, his version of a growl. Pebble knew he meant business. A passing hen took one look and decided the oak had grown a goat, which was close enough.

Task three: the bait. Pebble would curl near the cooling rack, pretending sleep, watching every shadow. His heart thumped like a drum.

The next Tuesday the plan sprang. Granny set four glorious buns out. Coral-the-banana perched. Moss stood guardian. Pebble curled, ears swivelling like radar.

Minutes stretched. A bee investigated Coral and left, disappointed. Granny hummed indoors, clattering a tray. Pebble’s whiskers inventoried every shadow: the drainpipe, the flour-sack, the place where crumbs went to think. Then a faint scritch-scratch from the bakery’s side. A shadow moved that was not a cloud. A badger with a determined look and a twitchy nose: Bartholomew. He had the walk of someone who had argued with himself all the way here and lost.

He crept toward the rack, nose vibrating with spice. He ignored the wobbly banana and the imposing goat. Eyes on the glistening buns. As he reached a paw, Pebble sprang.

“Gotcha.”

Coral, startled, shrieked, “Banana attack,” and fluttered at Bartholomew’s nose. What a commotion. The rivals of the morning — disguise, statue, bait — collided into one glorious tangle, and Bartholomew, surprised by noise and feathers, yelped and sat down, looking very embarrassed. Then he started to cry. Big badger tears.

“Why are you taking the buns?” Pebble asked, detective instincts softening.

Bartholomew sniffled. “It’s my little sister, Beatrice. She’s been feeling poorly. The only thing that makes her smile is Granny Buttercup’s spice buns. I haven’t managed enough acorns this week.”

Not a wicked thief. A worried brother.

“You should have asked,” Pebble said gently. “Granny is the kindest baker in the world.”

Coral perched on Moss. “She always shares.”

Moss nodded. “There’s always enough if we’re honest.”

Bartholomew wiped his eyes. “I was too shy. I didn’t want to bother anyone.”

Granny Buttercup, hearing the commotion, came out. She did not get cross. She gave him a cinnamon-scented hug. “You poor dear. Beatrice can have all the spice buns she needs.”

She packed a fresh bag for Beatrice, still warm, and tucked in an extra because poorly sisters sometimes want two smiles. She gave Pebble, Coral, and Moss one bun each, because they were such clever little detectives, even when their sting had caught a kindness. Pebble’s bun was so fragrant his knothole seemed, for a moment, unnecessary. Coral attempted to eat hers in character as a banana and got icing on her beak. Moss saved a crumb for later, which is how goats keep diaries.

Bartholomew took the buns home. Beatrice’s face lit. From that day he never stole again. He popped in, asked, and Granny always shared.

As for Pebble, he still peeks through the knothole on Tuesdays, whiskers first, as a professional courtesy to aroma. Sometimes he sees Bartholomew at the counter, paying in acorns and thanks. And if you ever hear a parrot practising being a banana, do not be alarmed. It is only Coral, keeping her disguise in working order, just in case the village ever needs another almost-mystery, and another almost-thief who only wanted a smile for someone small.
characters: Pebble (a pantry rat), Coral (a parrot), Moss (a goat)
